key_terms.meaning: σ = P/A, force P perpendicular to area A; tensile if pulling, compressive if pushing.
τ = V/A, force V parallel to area A.
ε = δ/L, change in length δ over original length L.
Highest stress up to which σ ∝ ε on the stress-strain curve.
Stress where noticeable plastic strain begins in a ductile material.
Maximum stress on the engineering stress-strain curve.
Ability to undergo large plastic strain before fracture, often measured by percentage elongation.
σ = E ε within the elastic limit.
FOS = failure stress / allowable working stress.
E = σ/ε in simple tension or compression.
G = τ/γ, shear stress over shear strain.
K = -Δp/(ΔV/V), pressure change over volumetric strain.
ε_v = ΔV/V = ε_x + ε_y + ε_z for small strains.
Two or more materials joined so they deform together and share load.
Axial member with more unknown reactions than equilibrium equations.
σ_th = E α ΔT for a fully restrained bar; α = coefficient of thermal expansion, ΔT = temperature change.
U = ½Pδ = σ²V/(2E) for gradual axial loading of volume V.
Dynamic maximum stress divided by static stress under the same load.

takeaways: Stress is internal force per unit area; normal stress acts perpendicular to a cut and shear stress acts along it.
A tension-test stress-strain curve reveals elastic limits, yield, ultimate strength and fracture, and separates ductile from brittle behaviour.
Hooke's law holds only within the elastic limit, and factor of safety converts a failure stress into a safe working stress.
For an isotropic elastic material, E, G, K and ν are connected, and only two of them are independent.
Volumetric strain is the sum of the three normal strains; for uniaxial stress ε_v = (σ/E)(1 - 2ν).
Axial deformation is δ = PL/(AE); compound bars share load while bonded parts share the same strain.
Statically indeterminate axial problems need compatibility of deformation in addition to equilibrium.
Thermal stress appears only when free thermal expansion or contraction is restrained.
Gradual axial loading stores U = ½Pδ, while sudden and impact loads produce larger maximum stress and strain energy.
bank_note: Long answers usually combine a labelled stress-strain or free-body sketch with equilibrium, compatibility and a numerical check, especially for compound, indeterminate and thermal cases.

bank.q: Define normal stress, shear stress and strain. Draw a typical tension-test stress-strain curve for a ductile material and label proportional limit, yield point, ultimate strength and fracture point; state what each label means.
outline: Axes: stress on y-axis, strain on x-axis
Difference between engineering curve and material behaviour

bank.q: State Hooke's law, define factor of safety, and explain why a working stress is lower than yield stress for a ductile material.
outline: Hooke's law σ = Eε and its elastic-limit condition
Reasons: material variability, load uncertainty, defects, fatigue
Working stress chosen below yield for safe design

bank.q: Define E, G, K and ν for an isotropic material. Explain why only two are independent and write the relation between E, G and ν.
outline: Definitions of E, G, K and ν
Isotropic meaning: same properties in all directions
Two independent constants for linear isotropic elasticity
Use of the constants in axial, shear and volumetric problems

bank.q: Explain, with sketches, deformation of a simple bar, a compound bar and a statically indeterminate axial member. State the equilibrium and compatibility equations used in each.
outline: Compound bar: common extension and load sharing
Indeterminate member: extra reaction and compatibility equation

bank.q: A steel rod 20 mm diameter and 2 m long carries an axial tensile load of 40 kN. Take E = 200 GPa. Find stress, strain, elongation and strain energy under gradual loading.

A compound bar made of steel and brass is bonded and carries an axial load P. Given the lengths, areas and E values, set up the equations for common extension, stresses in each material and load shared by each.
outline: Equilibrium P = σ_steel A_steel + σ_brass A_brass

bank.q: A bar fixed between two rigid walls is heated by ΔT. Derive the thermal stress and wall reaction. State how the answer changes if a small gap is left before the walls touch.
outline: Gap removes stress until gap closes

bank.q: A vertical steel rod is struck by a falling weight through a collar. Using strain energy, derive the maximum extension and maximum stress; state the assumptions.
outline: Loss of potential energy of weight
Assumptions: no energy loss, massless rod, valid elastic range

bank.q: A suddenly applied axial load P is put on a bar of length L, area A and modulus E. Compare the maximum stress and extension with the same load applied gradually; derive both results.
outline: Gradual load: σ = P/A, δ = PL/(AE)
Result P_max = 2P for suddenly applied load

bank.q: Compare ductile and brittle materials using stress-strain curves. Discuss how factor of safety choice differs and why elastic constants alone do not predict failure.
outline: Ductile curve: yield, large plastic strain, necking
Brittle curve: little plastic strain, sudden fracture
FOS based on yield for ductile and ultimate for brittle
Elastic constants describe stiffness, not strength
Role of defects, toughness and failure mode

bank.q: A composite member is constrained between rigid supports and loaded axially. Explain how to find reactions and interface stresses; identify why δ = PL/(AE) cannot be used alone.
outline: Different E and A for each part

bank.q: Evaluate the claim: 'A low Young's modulus material removes thermal stress.' Use σ_th = EαΔT for full restraint, and discuss strain energy and impact effects.
outline: Thermal stress proportional to E under full restraint
Low E lowers stress but may increase deformation

bank.q: Compare gradual, sudden and impact axial loading. Derive or state maximum stress factors and discuss assumptions about inertia, stress distribution and energy loss.
outline: Impact load: energy balance and impact factor
Assumptions: elastic behaviour, no losses, uniform stress

glossary.def: Internal force per unit area on a cut surface inside a material.
Stress acting perpendicular to the area on which it acts, either tensile or compressive.
Stress acting parallel to the area on which it acts.
Fractional change in length or shape produced by stress.
Property by which a material returns to its original shape after the load is removed.
Property by which a material undergoes permanent deformation without fracture.
Material that shows large plastic strain before breaking, such as mild steel.
Material that breaks with little plastic strain, such as cast iron.
Stress up to which stress and strain remain directly proportional.
Maximum stress up to which a material returns fully to its original shape.
Stress at which a material shows a specified small permanent strain.
Maximum engineering stress reached in a tension test.
Within the elastic limit, stress is proportional to strain.
Ratio of normal stress to normal strain in the elastic range.
Negative ratio of lateral strain to axial strain under axial loading.
Ratio of shear stress to shear strain in the elastic range.
Ratio of pressure change to volumetric strain with sign convention.
Fractional change in volume of a material element.
Bar made of two or more materials joined to act as one member.
Member whose reactions cannot be found from equilibrium alone.
Stress caused by prevented thermal expansion or contraction.
Energy stored in a deformed elastic member.
Strain energy absorbed in the elastic range without permanent deformation.
Load applied quickly by a moving body, producing dynamic stress and deformation.
Ratio of failure stress to allowable working stress.
Material whose elastic properties are the same in all directions.
